title: Dimensionality reduction with PCA
summary: Neuromatch W1D4 re-paced for a week: the geometric view of multivariate data (orthonormal bases, projections, variance along a direction), principal component analysis as the eigendecomposition of the sample covariance, variance explained and reconstruction error (the tutorials use MNIST images, not neural data), nonlinear embeddings with t-SNE and how to read them, and the interpretation question that matters for neuroscience: variance is not relevance.

objectives.description: Prove that the direction of maximal projected variance is the top eigenvector of the sample covariance, that successive components are uncorrelated, and compute components for a small covariance by hand.
Compute variance explained, cumulative variance and reconstruction error from eigenvalues, and choose a number of components with a stated criterion.

Explain the effects of centring and scaling, why variance explained is not information about a stimulus or behaviour, and give a counterexample where the relevant signal lives in a low-variance component.
Read a t-SNE embedding correctly (what it preserves and distorts) and distinguish the tutorials' synthetic Gaussian data and MNIST images from neural recordings.

preparation.description: W1D4 chapter page: Intro, Tutorials 1–4, Outro, day summary.
W1D4 Tutorial 1, Geometric view of data: simulated bivariate normal 'firing rates' of two neurons, an arbitrary orthonormal basis, projections.
W1D4 Tutorial 2, Principal Component Analysis: sample covariance, eigenvectors, projection S = XW, eigenvalues (simulated data).
W1D4 Tutorial 3, Dimensionality Reduction & Reconstruction: PCA on MNIST (70,000 handwritten-digit images, 784 pixels), variance explained, reconstruction, bonus denoising.
W1D4 Tutorial 4, Nonlinear Dimensionality Reduction: MNIST in two dimensions with PCA and t-SNE.

activities.title: Lesson: variance, bases and what they do not tell you
activities.instructions: Read the lesson before the notebooks. Do the two-dimensional eigen-decomposition in the lesson by hand before reading its solution. Note that none of the W1D4 datasets is a neural recording: Tutorials 1–2 simulate Gaussian 'firing rates' and Tutorials 3–4 use handwritten-digit images.

activities.title: Work through the W1D4 tutorials (Neuromatch notebooks)
activities.instructions: Run Tutorials 1–4 in the Neuromatch book (Colab or Kaggle; code BSD-3). Implement the covariance, eigendecomposition and projection yourself in Tutorial 2 before using library calls; keep the scree plot and the reconstructions from Tutorial 3; in Tutorial 4 change the t-SNE perplexity and record what moves.

activities.title: Tutorial: PCA proved and computed
activities.instructions: Attempt exercises 1 and 2 before asking for hints. Exercise 1 is a proof; write it for general dimension before the two-dimensional check. Exercise 2 is arithmetic on stated synthetic eigenvalues; the interpretation parts carry most of the weight.

activities.title: Explain: PCA on neural populations, synthetic data and images
activities.instructions: Exercise 3, written without the notes open.

activities.title: Retrieval: the unit's definitions
activities.instructions: From memory: the sample covariance for centred data; the variance of a projection; the eigen-characterisation of principal components; variance explained and cumulative variance; reconstruction error as the sum of discarded eigenvalues; what t-SNE preserves.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: the variance-maximisation characterisation proved for general dimension with the uncorrelatedness of components, and the two-dimensional case computed; and exercise 2 accepted with variance explained, reconstruction error and the variance-is-not-relevance counterexample.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The first principal components are the most informative dimensions of the population.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are the directions of largest variance. Variance can be noise, slow drift or a shared signal unrelated to the task; a behaviourally relevant signal can live in a low-variance component. Relevance needs a target variable; PCA has none.
Changing the units of one variable changes the covariance and the components. Centring is required for the covariance interpretation; scaling (correlation PCA) is a choice that must be stated.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Distances between clusters in a t-SNE plot measure how different the clusters are.
commonMisconceptions.correction: t-SNE preserves local neighbourhoods, not global distances; cluster sizes and inter-cluster distances depend on the perplexity and the random seed and should not be read quantitatively.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The W1D4 results are results about neurons.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Tutorials 1–2 use simulated Gaussian data standing in for two neurons' rates; Tutorials 3–4 use MNIST handwritten-digit images. The methods transfer to recordings; the results do not.

checks.name: source-locators
checks.evidence: W1D4 chapter page and Tutorials 1–4 opened 2026-10-30; objectives, section structure and data statements recorded: Tutorial 1 generates bivariate normal data as stand-ins for two neurons' firing rates; Tutorial 2 states Σ̂ = XᵀX/N for mean-subtracted data and S = XW, with 1000 samples from a zero-mean bivariate Gaussian; Tutorial 3 uses MNIST (70,000 images of 28 × 28 pixels); Tutorial 4 visualises the first 2,000 MNIST samples with PCA and t-SNE.

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Content agent re-derived: maximising wᵀΣw subject to ‖w‖ = 1 gives Σw = λw with variance λ (Lagrange multiplier or Rayleigh quotient); projections onto distinct eigenvectors have covariance w_iᵀΣw_j = λ_j w_iᵀw_j = 0. Σ = [[3, 1], [1, 3]]: eigenvalues 4 and 2, eigenvectors (1, 1)/√2 and (1, −1)/√2, PC1 share 4/6 = 66.7%. Eigenvalues 5.0, 2.5, 1.0, 0.8, 0.4, 0.3 (total 10.0): cumulative 50, 75, 85, 93, 97, 100%; reconstruction MSE with K components = Σ_{k>K} λ_k, so 2.5 for K = 2; K = 4 is the smallest with ≥ 90%. Lesson example Σ = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]: eigenvalues 3, 1, PC1 share 75%; eigenvalues 4, 3, 2, 1: K = 2 gives 70% and MSE 3.

checks.evidence: The lesson states the eigen-characterisation and the reconstruction-error identity but leaves the proofs to exercise 1; its covariance example ([[2, 1], [1, 2]]) and eigenvalue example (4, 3, 2, 1) differ from the exercises'. Reference reasoning only in instructor/.
